final_answer:
Endurance training elicits a PARTIAL but biologically structured coordinated molecular response across organs, and the two skeletal muscles (gastrocnemius and vastus lateralis) are by far the most similar tissues.

EXTENT OF COORDINATION (transcriptome, 19 tissues, 9,800 regulated genes):
- Roughly half of the training-regulated genes are shared across organs: 49.3% (4,831/9,800) are regulated in >=2 tissues, 24.2% in >=3, and 4.9% in >=5; the remaining 50.7% are regulated in a single tissue only. When a gene IS shared, its direction of change is usually consistent (mean 75.7% majority-direction agreement at 8w; 39.7% fully concordant).
- However, coordination is NOT uniform organism-wide: across all 107 tissue pairs the mean pairwise correlation of fold-changes is weak (r = 0.07-0.14 at each timepoint). Instead the coordinated signal is concentrated in a conserved "core" and in specific organ groups.
- The conserved core (genes regulated in >=6 tissues, 209 genes) is dominated by two programs: (1) mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation / energy metabolism (Mt-nd1/2/4/5/6, Mt-co1/co3, Mt-cyb, Mt-atp6, Cox4i1/5a/5b/6b/6c/7a2/7b, Ndufa3/6/11/12, Ndufb4/7/10/11, Ndufs3, Ndufv1, Uqcrbl1, Atp5f1a, Atp5mf, Atp5if1, Cycs, Coq9, Ucp2), which is UP in heart/kidney/liver/skeletal muscle but DOWN in adrenal and brown adipose; and (2) an immune/inflammatory program (Ptprc/CD45, Cd3e, Cd5, Cd6, Cd37, Cd63, Lck, Itk, Ikzf1/3, Bcl11b, Tyrobp, Lcp1, Lcp2, Itgb2, Cxcl9, Cxcl12, complement C1r/C1s/C3), largely DOWN in blood/spleen/lung/small-intestine.

MOST SIMILAR TISSUES:
1. Gastrocnemius (SKM-GN) and vastus lateralis (SKM-VL) - the two skeletal muscles - are the most similar pair by every measure, and the similarity GROWS with training duration: shared regulated genes n=218; Pearson correlation of fold-changes r = 0.78 (1w) -> 0.79 (2w) -> 0.87 (4w) -> 0.91 (8w), 95% CI [0.88, 0.93], Spearman 0.92 (p=2e-88); directional concordance 83% -> 96%; highest Jaccard set overlap (0.196). Their shared genes encode muscle contractile/structural proteins (Mybpc1, Mylk2, Tpm1, Pvalb, Flnc, Nrap, Dmd, Mb) plus an oxidative-metabolic module (Ckmt2, Ldha, Hk2, Fbp2, Pdhx and numerous mitochondrial OXPHOS subunits) - the canonical endurance-muscle adaptation.
2. Blood and spleen (r=0.78, n=338 shared genes, 90% concordance) - both immune-cell-rich tissues.
3. Adrenal (ADRNL) and brown adipose (BAT) (n=947 shared genes, 88% concordance).
The proteome independently corroborates a striated-muscle link: HEART and SKM-GN share the most proteins (199, 77% concordance).

BOTTOM LINE: Training produces a coordinated molecular response that is strongest within functionally related organs (skeletal muscle > immune tissues > adrenal/adipose), built on a shared mitochondrial/immune core whose direction differs between tissue groups, with gastrocnemius and vastus lateralis showing the most similar changes overall.

LIMITATION: The data contain only significantly regulated features (no unregulated background), so these similarities are computed on the shared-significant feature set and likely overstate absolute genome-wide correlation; cross-omic comparison is limited to the 7-8 tissues with protein/epigenetic data.
grader_notes: The analysis correctly used the 5% FDR transcriptome feature set and produced solid transcriptome similarity results, but it did not perform the required multi-assay, cross-assay aggregation and coverage-gap handling, so several cross-assay criteria are only partially met.

Expanded Tex-relevant TCR clonotypes shared across multiple patients (anti-PD-1-treated NSCLC cohort, GSE243013)

METHOD
- "Tex-relevant" = exhausted CD8+ T cells: sub_cell_type CD8T_Tex_HAVCR2 (TIM-3+) and CD8T_terminal_Tex_LAYN.
- "Expanded" = expansion == "expanded" (equivalent to clonotype_number >= 3).
- Clonotype identity reconstructed from the TCR sequence (the "clonotype" labels are patient-prefixed and cannot be compared across patients). Primary key = paired alpha+beta TCR (TRA_v_gene + TRA_cdr3 + TRB_v_gene + TRB_cdr3); beta-chain-only used as a sensitivity analysis.
- 434,458 T cells -> 41,337 Tex cells -> 34,053 expanded-Tex cells (221 patients) -> 5,578 unique paired clonotypes.

RESULT
Only 14 expanded-Tex clonotypes were found in >=2 patients (0 in >=3 patients), and these are dominated by two sample pairs with implausibly high total TCR overlap (a contamination/mislabeling signature, not independent patients):

1. P199 & P200 share 12 of the 14 clonotypes (and 123 full TCRs overall vs. a cohort background of median 1, p99 = 3 per sample pair). Examples:
   - TRAV12-3 | CAMSDLGAGAGSYQLTF | TRBV5-5 | CASSPGPGGTEAFF (59 cells)
   - TRAV13-1 | CAAEMDSNYQLIW | TRBV6-2 | CASSVSGTGFLRQPQHF (37 cells)
   - TRAV29/DV5 | CAASDNWVSSTSYGKLTF | TRBV19 | CASSMTSGPGETQYF (23 cells)
2. P70 & P71 share the other 2 clonotypes (29 full TCRs overall):
   - TRAV8-1 | CAVKNTGGFKTIF | TRBV27 | CASSLAGGDEQYF (246 cells; largest shared clone)
   - TRAV24 | CALIIGFGNVLHC | TRBV4-3 | CASSPTGTGLEGYTF (40 cells)

After excluding these two contamination-driven pairs, only ONE paired clonotype remains shared across two patients:
   - TRAV12-1 | CVVNPNTDKLIF | TRBV20-1 | CSASVGSYEQYF (6 cells; P391 [nPR] and P482 [pPR], 3 cells each).
Beta-chain-only shared clonotypes outside the outlier pairs are similarly sparse: TRBV7-2|CASSSGGYEQYF and TRBV20-1|CSASVGSYEQYF (P391/P482), TRBV7-9|CASSDSLSSYNEQFF (P45/P5), TRBV29-1|CSVGTGGTNEKLFF (P124/P520) — all 2-patient overlaps within the chance background.

CONCLUSION / CANDIDATES
There is no high-confidence expanded-Tex TCR clonotype that genuinely recurs across multiple independent patients in this dataset. The apparent sharing is almost entirely a cross-sample contamination artifact (P199/P200 and P70/P71), so those clonotypes should NOT be proposed as public TCR-T candidates without orthogonal verification (e.g. wet-lab antigen screen). The only sequence that survives the contamination filter and is shared between two distinct patients at the paired-alpha-beta level is TRAV12-1|CVVNPNTDKLIF|TRBV20-1|CSASVGSYEQYF (P391 & P482), and it is consistent with background public-TCR convergence (not found in a third patient), so it is only a weak, tentative candidate. Reaching the bar for a TCR-T therapy candidate would require recurrence in >=3 independent patients and/or demonstrated shared tumor-antigen specificity, which these data do not provide.
grader_notes: The agent performed data loading and cross-patient sharing analysis but deviated from the exact expanded_terminal_Tex subset, omitted J genes and the >=10-cell per-patient filter, did not prioritise MPR, and lacked concrete validation criteria.

QUESTION
Which plasma proteins are significantly altered after 6 months of feminizing GAHT, and do the changes differ between the CPA and SPIRO antiandrogen regimens?

ANSWER

METHOD (summary)
Recomputed associations from the raw Olink Explore-HT NPX table (data/Olink_CPA_SPIRO_GAHT_and_pregnancy.npx.csv; 5,416 proteins, 20 CPA + 20 SPIRO subjects with complete baseline and 6-month pairs). Timepoint was read from the sample-name suffix (_0m vs _6m) and cross-checked against the NPX Group_Name1 column (this fixes four mislabeled SPIRO rows in the SDRF metadata). For each protein I computed the within-subject change d = NPX(6m) - NPX(0m) and tested it with a one-sample t-test (equivalent to a mixed model with a per-subject random intercept for this balanced two-timepoint design; verified against statsmodels.MixedLM). Regimen differences were tested with a Welch two-sample t-test on d (the time x regimen interaction). P-values were Benjamini-Hochberg corrected (FDR < 0.05). All 103 study samples passed SampleQC and had complete NPX.

1) PROTEINS SIGNIFICANTLY ALTERED AFTER 6 MONTHS OF GAHT
Overall (CPA + SPIRO pooled, n = 40 subjects): 569 proteins were significantly altered (BH-FDR < 0.05); 550 decreased and 19 increased.

The response is dominated by down-regulation of male-reproductive / androgen-dependent proteins, e.g. (mean log2 change):
  SPINT3 -5.71, INSL3 -3.55, EDDM3B -1.99, TEX101 -1.49, MSMB -0.72, plus ACRV1, DEFB4A/B, SPATA2L, PROK1, MUC1, CA6, SPINK2, SPINK5, MUC7, PGLYRP3, VIT.
A smaller set of estrogen-responsive proteins increased (19 up-regulated):
  LEP +1.27, CXCL13 +1.03, OXT +0.82, PRL +0.79, SERPINA12 +0.72, NT-proBNP +0.64, PZP +0.40, LPL +0.39, SHBG +0.29, CSF3, PAEP, CCL28, CST7, ASAH2, TNFAIP6, FOLR3, VEGFD, MZB1, CD70.

By regimen:
  - CPA (n = 20): 265 significant proteins (12 up, 253 down).
  - SPIRO (n = 20): 118 significant proteins (2 up [LEP, IL5RA], 116 down).

2) DO THE CHANGES DIFFER BETWEEN CPA AND SPIRO?
Yes. The 6-month changes are concordant in direction for 567/569 (99.6%) of overall-significant proteins, but CPA produces a LARGER and BROADER response, and 10 proteins show a statistically significant regimen difference (BH-FDR < 0.05):

  INSL3   CPA -5.34 vs SPIRO -1.75   (testicular suppression stronger on CPA)
  PRL     CPA +1.38 vs SPIRO +0.19   (prolactin rise essentially CPA-specific)
  NELL1   CPA +0.21 vs SPIRO -0.23   (opposite directions)
  SPINT3  CPA -7.91 vs SPIRO -3.52   (stronger on CPA)
  CXCL13  CPA +1.84 vs SPIRO +0.21   (larger rise on CPA)
  CFC1    CPA +0.57 vs SPIRO -0.16   (opposite directions)
  SPOCK1  CPA -0.34 vs SPIRO -0.05   (larger drop on CPA)
  RTBDN   CPA -0.44 vs SPIRO -0.02   (larger drop on CPA)
  EDDM3B  CPA -2.67 vs SPIRO -1.32   (stronger on CPA)
  REN     CPA -0.56 vs SPIRO +0.19   (renin rises on SPIRO, falls on CPA)

INTERPRETATION
Both regimens produce the expected feminizing proteomic signature: loss of androgen/testis-driven proteins (MSMB, INSL3, TEX101, EDDM3B, SPINT3) and induction of estrogen-driven proteins (SHBG, prolactin, leptin, PZP, LPL). CPA (a potent progestin + antiandrogen) suppresses the gonadal axis more completely, giving larger drops in testicular proteins and a larger prolactin rise, whereas SPIRO (a weaker antiandrogen but a mineralocorticoid-receptor antagonist) has a smaller suppressive effect and a regimen-specific RENIN INCREASE consistent with its aldosterone-blocking activity.

LIMITATIONS
CPA and SPIRO samples were run in separate batches (run 1 vs run 2), so absolute protein levels cannot be compared across regimens; the paired change (and its between-regimen comparison) is used to remove additive batch effects. n = 20 per regimen limits power, so only 10 proteins survive FDR correction for the regimen difference (311 are significant at nominal p<0.05). Olink NPX is relative (log2) quantification, and only the 5,416 assays on the panel could be tested. Full per-protein results are in results_GAHT_CPA_SPIRO.tsv.
grader_notes: The analysis is statistically rigorous and biologically insightful, with correct data handling, paired testing, multiple testing correction, and interpretation; the main gap is the lack of explicit unique/shared protein set quantification between regimens.

Synthetic-lethal partner predictions for loss-of-function (LOF) events in BRCA
================================================================================

Approach summary: I combined (1) lasso regression of gene essentiality (DepMap
CRISPR dependency) on damaging-mutation features in the 36 BRCA cell lines that
have both mutation and dependency data, (2) pairwise mutual-exclusivity testing
(Fisher exact) across recurrently mutated genes in the 74-cell-line BRCA
mutation matrix, and (3) paralog (Ensembl Compara) and protein-protein
interaction (STRING, score >= 700) priors. Candidates were ranked by a composite
of effect size, statistical significance, and prior strength, then ordered for
translational relevance (druggability + clinical precedent + LOF-event
prevalence).

Mutual-exclusivity testing yielded no significant pairs (all BH-FDR = 1.0),
because the synthetic-lethal partners are essential genes that are essentially
never themselves mutated (PARP1 1/74, PIK3CB 0/74, SMARCA2 0/74, SMARCA4 0/74,
FEN1 0/74, RAF1 0/74). The ranking therefore rests on the lasso + paralog/PPI
priors.

RANKED SYNTHETIC-LETHAL PARTNER CANDIDATES
------------------------------------------
(effect = mean dependency shift, mutant minus wild-type; negative = stronger
essentiality in mutant lines, i.e. the SL direction)

1. PTEN LOF -> PIK3CB (p110-beta catalytic subunit of PI3K)
   - Lasso + Wilcoxon: effect -0.435, p = 5.1e-4 (strongest hit)
   - Prior: direct PTEN-PIK3CB PPI (PI3K complex)
   - Mechanism: PTEN loss hyperactivates PI3K/AKT; p110-beta becomes rate-limiting.
   - Translational: p110-beta-selective inhibitors (e.g. AZD6482) are selectively
     active in PTEN-null tumors (validated SL; Jia 2008, Wee 2008).

2. BRCA1 LOF -> PARP1
   - Lasso + Wilcoxon: effect -0.201, p = 0.092 (direction consistent)
   - Prior: PARP1 in the BRCA1 HR-repair network (STRING)
   - Mechanism: HR-deficient BRCA1-mutant cells depend on PARP-mediated repair.
   - Translational: clinically validated; FDA-approved PARP inhibitors
     (olaparib/talazoparib/niraparib/rucaparib) (Bryant 2005, Farmer 2005).

3. ARID1A LOF -> ARID1B
   - Lasso + Wilcoxon: effect -0.327, p = 0.114 (direction consistent)
   - Prior: PARALOG (48.9% identity) + PPI (same SWI/SNF complex)
   - Mechanism: paralog redundancy; ARID1A loss creates dependence on ARID1B.
   - Translational: validated paralog SL (Helming 2014); ARID1B is a hard-to-drug
     TF, targetable indirectly (e.g. via EZH2/HDAC).

4. ARID1A LOF -> SMARCA4 (BRG1) and SMARCA2 (BRM)
   - Lasso + Wilcoxon: SMARCA4 effect -0.306, p = 0.049; SMARCA2 effect -0.152,
     p = 0.041
   - Prior: PPI (SWI/SNF ATPases)
   - Translational: SMARCA2/4 PROTAC degraders in development (Hoffman 2014, Oike 2013).
   - Patient-level support: SMARCA4 is predicted essential in 23% of 2,372 TCGA
     BRCA patients, consistent with a patient subset depending on SWI/SNF.

5. BRCA2 LOF -> FEN1
   - Lasso + Wilcoxon: effect -0.318, p = 0.066
   - Prior: PPI (HR / flap-endonuclease pathway)
   - Translational: FEN1 inhibitors in development (Mengwasser 2019).

6. TP53 LOF -> PARP1
   - Lasso + Wilcoxon: effect -0.150, p = 0.044
   - Mechanism: TP53 loss impairs HR, sensitizing to PARP inhibition.
   - Note: TP53 is mutated in 27/36 lines, so this may partly reflect general
     TP53-mutant cell-line state.

7. NF1 LOF -> RAF1
   - Lasso + Wilcoxon: effect -0.235, p = 0.12
   - Prior: PPI (RAS-MAPK pathway)
   - Translational: RAF/MEK-pathway inhibitors.

8. BRCA1 LOF -> additional HR-repair partners (RAD50, FANCI, RBBP8, RFC2, NBN)
   - Lasso: effects -0.16 to -0.36, p = 0.003-0.10; all PPI members of the
     BRCA1 DNA-repair complex; preclinical DNA-repair targets.

BOTTOM LINE
-----------
The analysis recovers the canonical, clinically validated BRCA synthetic
lethalities (BRCA1/2 -> PARP1) and two additional high-confidence, druggable
candidates: PTEN -> PIK3CB (p110-beta) and ARID1A -> ARID1B/SMARCA2 (SWI/SNF
paralog/complex), plus BRCA2 -> FEN1 and NF1 -> RAF1.

Caveats: n = 36 cell lines (per-event mutant n = 3-27); no single pair survives
genome-wide multiple-testing correction; the damaging-mutation matrix is
cell-line (CCLE) not patient data; mutual exclusivity was uninformative; and
patient dependency scores are model-predicted and cover only 1,966 genes.
The list is therefore a hypothesis-generating, mechanism-prioritized ranking
rather than a confirmatory result.
grader_notes: The analysis implemented lasso with BIC-selected lambda, mutual-exclusivity testing, and paralog/PPI/literature integration, but lacked CV-based lambda selection, dual-threshold refinement, iterative mutual-exclusivity prioritization, canonical paralog pair reporting, and observed-vs-expected co-occurrence reporting.

Yes. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) identifies modules of co-expressed genes in ALS spinal cord, and those modules resolve into coordinated gene programs whose ALS dysregulation is reproducible across spinal levels.

What was done
- Built an unsigned co-expression network from the cervical spinal cord (174 samples: 138 ALS, 36 control) using the 8,000 most variable genes (log2 TPM, soft-threshold power 20, truncated scale-free R2 = 0.85; TOM + average-linkage clustering + dynamic tree cut, min module size 30, merge cutHeight 0.25).
- Detected 6 modules; associated each module eigengene with ALS status using a linear model adjusted for age, sex, RIN, and sequencing platform.

Key findings
1. Glial/immune activation — module "grey60" (71 genes) is UPREGULATED in ALS (covariate-adjusted p = 1.3e-9). Its hub genes are microglia/macrophage markers (CTSS, MSR1, LY86, CD74, C3AR1, FCER1G, HLA-DRA/DMA/DMB/DPA1) enriched for translation/ribosome and MHC class II antigen presentation. This signature is also elevated in ALS in lumbar (p = 7e-7) and thoracic (p = 0.049) spinal cord.
2. Neuronal/synaptic loss — module "lightyellow" (366 genes) is DOWN in ALS (p = 2.9e-3), enriched for synaptic transmission, with hubs SHANK1, SYN3, BSN, UNC13A.
3. Vascular/endothelial loss — module "purple" (139 genes) is DOWN in ALS (p = 4.3e-3), enriched for angiogenesis (VWF, TIE1, ROBO4, DLL4, ESAM).
4. A mixed "cyan" module (883 genes, p = 9.9e-6) containing oligodendrocyte-lineage genes (MYRF, ABCA2) is DOWN in ALS and replicates in lumbar (p = 7.3e-3).

Orthogonal validation (independent of WGCNA, using Mathys et al. 2019 cell-type markers) confirms the same direction: microglia are increased (+0.27, p = 1.8e-3) and oligodendrocytes decreased (-0.41, p = 8.9e-5) in ALS cervical cord, with both replicated in lumbar.

Conclusion
WGCNA successfully identifies co-expression modules in ALS spinal cord; the coordinated programs most robustly dysregulated in ALS are microglial/immune activation (up) together with neuronal, oligodendrocyte, and vascular programs (down) — a signature consistent with glial activation and neurodegeneration. The main caveat is that bulk tissue cannot fully separate gene-level dysregulation from altered cell-type composition, which is why the findings were cross-checked with marker-based cell-type scoring.
grader_notes: The agent performed a competent WGCNA analysis with clear biological interpretation, but included controls in the network (violating the ALS-only requirement), used unsigned power 20 instead of signed power ~8, and did not fully correct for batch effects, leading to several B/C ratings on rubric criteria.

METHOD: I analyzed the 576 DMSO-vehicle ("Ginkgo Neg Control - DMSO") baseline samples (144 per cell type; 573 after removing 3 failed AoSMC libraries) from GDPx2-GeneCounts.h5, normalizing to log2(CPM+1) over 18,241 expressed genes and focusing PCA on the top 2,000 highly variable genes. 1) Distinct, not overlapping. The 573 baseline samples separate into four tight, non-overlapping clusters: PCA PC1/PC2/PC3 = 41.8% / 26.6% / 20.2% of variance encode the four-group structure; silhouette score = 0.86 (0.84-0.88 per type); a 5-fold cross-validated k-NN(5) classifier predicts cell type with 100% accuracy (perfectly diagonal confusion matrix); 100% of samples' transcriptomic nearest neighbor is the same cell type; mean within-type Spearman correlation 0.92 vs 0.81 between types, and every sample correlates more with its own centroid (mean 0.95) than with any other centroid (best-other 0.85).
2) Lineage-structured overlap and most-similar pairs. The three mesoderm-derived mesenchymal types are mutually closer than any is to the neural-crest-derived melanocyte. Centroid Spearman correlations: SkMM-fibroblast 0.902 (highest), AoSMC-SkMM 0.876, AoSMC-fibroblast 0.869, melanocyte-others 0.811-0.839. Hierarchical clustering gives ((AoSMC, (SkMM, fibroblast)), melanocyte).
3) MOST SIMILAR: skeletal muscle myoblasts (SkMM) and dermal fibroblasts (Spearman 0.902, Pearson 0.924), consistent with shared mesenchymal/myofibroblast identity (both express ACTA2, TAGLN, CNN1, MYOCD and collagen genes).
4) MOST DISTINCT: melanocytes (outgroup), defined by an exclusive melanocyte program (MLANA, PMEL, DCT, TYR, TYRP1, SLC45A2, MITF, SOX10) essentially absent in the other three types.
5) Marker signatures: myoblasts = MYOD1, MYF5, DES; fibroblasts = DCN, S100A4, PDGFRA, FBLN1, TNC; AoSMC = an inflammatory/secretory program (IL1B, IL6, CXCL6, SFRP4, CD24) with LOW canonical contractile markers (ACTA2, MYH11, MYOCD), indicating a synthetic/dedifferentiated in-vitro SMC phenotype; melanocytes = melanosomal/lineage program above.

CONCLUSION: The four primary cell types have clearly distinct baseline transcriptional signatures (strongly separated, ~100% classifiable), so cell identity dominates the platform's variation. They are most similar in a lineage-consistent way: myoblasts and dermal fibroblasts are the most similar pair, AoSMC is the next-closest mesenchymal relative, and melanocytes are the most distinct (neural-crest lineage). Caveats: "baseline" is the 24-h DMSO vehicle; the AoSMC profile reflects cultured (synthetic/pro-inflammatory) smooth muscle cells; and marker differential expression was not genome-wide FDR-controlled.

For each of 7 predictors (PLAAC, PScore, catGRANULE, SaPS-8fea, SaPS-10fea, PdPS-8fea, PdPS-10fea) and each of 6 membership datasets, I measured "screening performance" as the ROC AUC of ranking that dataset's members above the fixed non-PS background (hNoPS, n=8,801), using the de-overlapped "Training proteins removed" sheet. I then compared MLO datasets (OpenCell nuclear punctae, DACT1 particulate proteome, G3BP1 proximity labeling, PhaSepDB high-throughput) against the membrane-bound control (Proteomics of human mitochondria), and also tested MLO vs mitochondria directly (Mann-Whitney U).

Key results.
1. Screening AUC vs the hNoPS background: the SaPS/PdPS classifiers rank MLO datasets strongly (AUC 0.63-0.84; best PdPS-10fea on G3BP1 = 0.839, DACT1 = 0.832), catGRANULE is intermediate (0.55-0.72), while the mitochondrial control gives much lower AUCs for the same predictors (SaPS/PdPS: 0.47-0.56; catGRANULE 0.52, near chance). PLAAC and PScore are weak screeners overall (most AUCs <= 0.52).
2. Consistency: all 7 predictors yield a higher mean MLO AUC than the membrane AUC (mean difference +0.15); a paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test is significant (p = 0.0078, W = 28). The mitochondrial set ranks last or second-to-last among all 6 datasets for 6 of 7 predictors.
3. Direct contrast: pooled MLO members score significantly higher than mitochondrial proteins for every predictor (Mann-Whitney p from 4.1e-06 to 8.2e-107; discrimination AUC 0.55 for PLAAC up to 0.74 for PdPS-10fea). A top-10% screen recovers ~14-39% of MLO members but only ~3-8% of mitochondrial proteins (mitochondria are depleted from the top of the PS scores).

Interpretation. Predictors — especially the supervised SaPS/PdPS classifiers and, to a lesser extent, catGRANULE — are specific for phase-separating/MLO biology: they enrich MLO participants over a non-PS background but do not enrich membrane-bound organelle residents. The amyloid-fiber control (a self-assembling aggregate, not an MLO) is intermediate and not significantly better screened than mitochondria (p = 0.19), confirming the signal is not a generic property of any self-assembling set.

Caveats. (i) The MLO > membrane ordering holds for all 7 predictors, but PLAAC and PScore are near-chance on most sets, so "better" is a relative comparison, not an endorsement of every predictor's absolute power. (ii) hNoPS is "non-SaPS/non-PdPS" rather than functionally non-PS and overlaps some MLO members (excluded from negatives per-dataset). (iii) PhaSepDB high-throughput is only 1,712/2,415 human-scorable. (iv) OpenCell (115) and Amyloid (62) positives are small, making their AUCs noisier. (v) AUC vs a fixed background is relative and does not give an absolute screening threshold.

Top signaling pathways (beyond the established MHC-I interaction) predicted to mediate the suppressive function and cytotoxic targeting of KIR+CD8+ T cells against pathogenic gliadin-specific CD4+ T cells in celiac-disease inflamed tissue.

Analysis: 10 single-cell count matrices (GSE193442; 6 CeD, 4 HC) were merged, QC-filtered (72,177 -> 67,286 cells), clustered (Leiden), and cell types assigned by marker rules. KIR+CD8+ T cells (CD3+ CD8+ and any KIR UMI: KIR2DL1/2DL3/3DL1/3DL2/3DL3/2DL4/3DX1) = 1,018 cells in CeD; pathogenic CD4+ T cells were proxied by activated CD4+ T cells (CD4+ and IL2RA/CD69/CD38+) = 3,778 cells. Cell-cell communication was inferred with CellChat v2.1.2 (CellChatDB.human, triMean, nboot=100 permutation) on the CeD T/NK compartment, and the cytotoxic/suppressive effector program was quantified directly because CellChatDB omits granule proteins.

ANSWER

The dominant interaction is MHC-I (HLA-A/B/C/E/F -> CD8A/CD8B, KIR3DL1, KIR2DL3; netP probability 2.28, Activated CD4 T -> KIR+CD8 T), which corresponds to the established recognition axis (HLA-E and KIR/HLA-C) and was therefore set aside. Beyond MHC-I, the top predicted pathways are:

1) Cytotoxic targeting — granzyme/perforin + FASL/FAS death-receptor program (the strongest effector signal, measured directly because these are not CellChatDB L-R pairs):
   - GZMA (91% of KIR+CD8 T), GZMB (82%), GZMH (86%), PRF1/perforin (91%), LAMP1 (49%) — a near-uniform cytolytic program, far above non-KIR CD8 T cells (GZMB 16%, PRF1 37%).
   - FASLG-FAS: FASLG enriched on KIR+CD8 T (8.7% vs 2.4% non-KIR CD8 T), FAS on activated CD4 T (8.0%) — death-receptor killing.
   - Granzyme A -> PAR-1 (the CellChat "PARs" pathway, GZMA->F2R) is significant (p<0.05), a pro-inflammatory/apoptotic signal.

2) Chemokine targeting — CCL5/RANTES (98%) and CCL4/MIP-1b (78%) secreted by KIR+CD8 T (vs 52%/25% in non-KIR CD8 T), predicted to recruit and colocalize CCR5/CCR1-expressing pathogenic CD4 T cells.

3) Suppressive signaling — TGFB1 (53% of KIR+CD8 T) signaling to TGFBR2 on CD4 T, and the co-inhibitory checkpoint module TIGIT (28%) and LAG3 (19%), elevated relative to non-KIR CD8 T. IL-10 is not a mediator (0% of cells).

4) CellChat-significant adhesion/co-signaling and recognition-reinforcement pathways (all p<0.05):
   - MIF (MIF -> CD74/CD44, CD74/CXCR4; prob 0.270, Activated CD4 T -> KIR+CD8 T)
   - LCK (LCK -> CD8 receptor; prob 0.149)
   - CD99 (CD99-CD99; prob 0.139, bidirectional)
   - CypA (PPIA -> BSG/CD147; prob 0.133/0.050)
   - SELPLG (PSGL-1 -> SELL; prob 0.113, KIR+CD8 T -> CD4 T)
   - CLEC (CD69 -> KLRB1/CD161; CLEC2D/2B -> KLRB1; prob 0.061, Activated CD4 T -> KIR+CD8 T) — the activated CD69+ pathogenic CD4 T cell engages CD161 on the KIR+CD8 T cell
   - ICAM (ICAM2 -> LFA-1/ITGAL-ITGB2; prob 0.017)
   - SIRP (SIRPG -> CD47; prob 0.006)
   - IL16 (IL16 -> CD4; prob 0.029) and MHC-II (HLA-DPA1/DPB1/DRB1 -> CD4; prob 0.178), from KIR+CD8 T to CD4 T.

In summary, the suppressive/cytotoxic function is best attributed to (1) the granzyme/perforin + FASL cytolytic program and the granzyme A-PARs axis for direct killing, (2) CCL5/CCL4 chemokines for targeting/recruitment, and (3) TGF-beta plus the TIGIT/LAG3 checkpoint module for suppression, with MIF, LCK-CD8, CD99, CD69-KLRB1 (CLEC), ICAM/LFA-1 and SIRPG-CD47 as the significant non-MHC-I communication pathways that reinforce recognition, adhesion, and co-signaling. Caveats: gliadin specificity is a TCR property absent from these data (activated CD4+ T cells were used as proxy), and CCR5 detection is limited by scRNA drop-out.

Yes — GAHT-induced plasma-protein changes are broadly consistent with those observed during menopausal hormone therapy (MHT), and they are the directional mirror image of the menopausal transition. The consistency is driven by their shared hormonal mediator (estradiol), but GAHT also has a testosterone-suppression component that MHT does not reproduce.

Key quantitative findings (from the 258 GAHT-associated proteins, 245 down / 13 up):

1. GAHT vs MHT — concordant direction.
   - 80.2% (207/258) of GAHT proteins change in the same direction as MHT in the age >=57 stratum (binomial p = 1.8e-23); 72.1% in the <57 stratum (p = 8.5e-13).
   - GAHT proteins are 2.7-fold over-represented among MHT-significant proteins (Fisher OR 5.08, p = 6.6e-30); 92% of the overlapping proteins are directionally concordant.
   - Proteome-wide, GAHT and MHT effect sizes are positively correlated (Spearman rho = +0.11, p = 6e-9).

2. GAHT vs menopause — opposite direction (GAHT = anti-menopause).
   - 85.3% (220/258) of GAHT proteins change opposite to the early menopause (<57) transition (p = 2.5e-32); proteome-wide rho = -0.32 (p = 9e-68).
   - (The menopause >=57 stratum is uninformative — only 3 significant proteins there — so the <57 stratum is the valid comparator.)

3. Mechanism — the changes track the sex hormones.
   - 72.1% of GAHT proteins are directionally consistent with estradiol (p = 8.5e-13) and 69.0% anti-consistent with testosterone (p = 9.8e-10), matching GAHT's profile (raises estradiol, lowers testosterone).

4. Important caveat — a GAHT-specific androgen axis.
   - 95% of GAHT proteins are down-regulated, led by testis/epididymis-specific factors (SPINT3, INSL3, EDDM3B, TEX101, ACRV1, MSMB) that fall with androgen suppression. These have no counterpart in MHT/menopause (non-significant there), which explains the ~20% that are not MHT-concordant. The shared estrogen axis is carried by classic estrogen targets (e.g., prolactin PRL and leptin LEP rise with both GAHT and MHT).

Conclusion: GAHT reproduces the proteomic signature of estrogen therapy (consistent with MHT) and reverses the signature of the menopausal estrogen decline, confirming estradiol as the common driver. However, the agreement is directional rather than quantitative (modest effect-size correlations), and GAHT additionally includes an anti-androgen-driven down-regulation of testis-derived proteins that MHT does not model, so the two signatures are not identical.

Tumor mutational load is NUMERICALLY higher in anti-PD-1 responders, but the association is NOT statistically significant in this cohort (n = 38: 21 responders [R], 17 non-responders [NR]).

PRIMARY RESULT (non-synonymous SNVs, "TotalNonSyn" — the standard tumor mutational burden measure):
- Responders: median 495 nsSNVs (IQR 313-807), mean 817.9.
- Non-responders: median 281 nsSNVs (IQR 232-621), mean 536.8.
- Statistical test: two-sided Mann-Whitney U (Wilcoxon rank-sum) test — chosen because mutation counts are strongly right-skewed and non-normal in both groups (Shapiro-Wilk p < 0.01).
- Result: U = 214.0, p = 0.304 (confirmed by 200,000-iteration permutation test, p ~ 0.305). NOT significant at alpha = 0.05.
- Effect size / association metrics: Cliff's delta = 0.199 (small effect); rank-biserial/Spearman rho = 0.17; P(responder load > non-responder load) = 0.599.

CONSISTENCY ACROSS OTHER LOAD MEASURES (all non-significant, responders higher):
- Total SNVs (including silent/non-coding): R 2976 vs NR 1942, U = 226, p = 0.168.
- Non-synonymous indels: R 3 vs NR 2, p = 0.171.
- Expressed nsSNVs: p = 0.628; neoepitope Binder: p = 0.411.
- Logistic regression (Response ~ log2 load): odds ratio = 1.365 per doubling of load (95% CI 0.84-2.23), p = 0.213.

ORDINAL TREND (irRECIST categories): median load increases monotonically with response depth — Progressive Disease 281 -> Partial Response 463 -> Complete Response 668 (Jonckheere-Terpstra trend test, one-sided p = 0.093).

CONCLUSION: Higher tumor mutational load trends toward a higher likelihood and deeper response to anti-PD-1, but this association does not reach statistical significance in this 38-patient melanoma cohort. We therefore fail to reject the null hypothesis of no association; the effect is small (Cliff's delta ~0.20) and the study is likely underpowered to detect a modest effect.

Yes. Non-Negative Matrix Factorization (NMF) of the tumor immune microenvironment composition identifies an optimal 3-class patient classification.

WHAT WAS DONE
- Built a 243-patient x 51-immune-cell-state composition matrix (per-patient proportions of sub_cell_type labels) from the 1,254,749-cell metadata (GSE243013).
- Ran consensus NMF for ranks k = 2..12 (30 random restarts per k) and selected the optimal rank using the standard consensus criteria: Brunet cophenetic correlation, Kim-Park dispersion, and cross-restart stability (mean pairwise ARI).

OPTIMAL RANK: k = 3
- Cophenetic correlation peaks at k=3 (0.958) with a sharp drop at k=4 (0.864).
- Dispersion peaks at k=3 (0.684); mean pairwise ARI peaks at k=3 (0.660).
- All three consensus metrics agree on k=3, the most reproducible partition.

THE OPTIMAL CLASSIFICATION (3 NMF classes)
1. "T-cell-rich" class (n=127; 58/126 = 46.0% MPR+ among those with response annotation): dominated by CD8 memory/effector (CD8T_Tm_IL7R, CD8T_Tem_GZMK+GZMH+), Treg (CD4T_Treg_FOXP3), exhausted CD8 (CD8T_Tex_CXCL13).
2. "B-cell-rich" class (n=86; 55/86 = 64.0% MPR+): dominated by memory B cells (Bm_PDE4D, Bm_TNFSF9, Bm_TNF), plasma cells, naive B (Bn_TCL1A).
3. "Myeloid-rich" class (n=30; 17/30 = 56.7% MPR+): dominated by macrophages (Mφ_MARCO, Mφ_VCAN, Mφ_FOLR2), neutrophils (Neu_FCGR3B), NK (NK_CD16hi_FGFBP2).

The classes associate with pathological response: B-cell-rich patients have the highest MPR rate (64.0% vs 46.0% for T-cell-rich), significantly higher than the T-cell-rich class (class x MPR+/non-MPR chi2 = 6.72, p = 0.035; pairwise Fisher OR = 0.48, p = 0.012). The classification is unsupervised and the response association is exploratory (not adjusted for other clinical covariates); silhouette values are low (<=0.29), so the classes are best read as "dominant TIME programs" rather than sharply separated clusters; and the k=3 optimum is specific to the proportional scale (aggressive re-scaling shifts it toward k=2).

Amino-acid composition: PS-Self (SaPS) vs PS-Part (PdPS)
=======================================================

SaPS (self-assembling) proteins are compositionally distinct from PdPS
(partner-dependent) proteins. On the human sets (hSaPS n=59 vs hPdPS n=96),
hSaPS proteins are significantly enriched in glycine (median 8.1% vs 6.5%,
+25%; FDR q=0.005), while hPdPS proteins are significantly enriched in
glutamate (7.9% vs 5.8%, q=0.009), leucine (8.8% vs 7.1%, q=0.005) and lysine
(6.4% vs 4.8%, q=0.013). The larger cross-organism sets (SaPS n=128 vs PdPS
n=214) reproduce and sharpen this picture: SaPS are enriched in disorder-
promoting residues G, P, S, Q; PdPS are enriched in the charged residues
E, K, R, D and the hydrophobic residues L, I, V (plus H and C), all FDR<0.05.
By chemical class, PS-Self proteins carry more polar-uncharged (S/T/N/Q)
residues and more glycine/proline, whereas PS-Part proteins carry more charged
residues (both acidic and basic) and more aliphatic hydrophobics. Within
intrinsically disordered regions (IDR-restricted), SaPS are further enriched in
glutamine and phenylalanine (Q +0.014 q=0.002; F +0.008 ~2-fold, q=0.0007,
cross-organism), with lower glutamate/lysine — consistent with glutamine/
aromatic "sticker" residues driving self-assembly, while PdPS IDRs retain more
charged residues. Interpretation: SaPS have the signature of disordered, sticky
scaffolds; PdPS are closer to charged, partner-dependent "clients" whose
condensation depends on heterotypic interactions rather than autonomous
self-assembly.

Predictor performance (distinguishing each PS type from non-PS)
===============================================================

Three of the four named predictors are present in the data (PScore, PLAAC,
catGRANULE); FuzDrop scores are NOT provided and therefore could not be
evaluated (no FuzDrop column anywhere in the workspace files).

All three available predictors discriminate SaPS from NoPS well, but are much
weaker at discriminating PdPS from NoPS:

  SaPS vs NoPS (ROC-AUC):  PScore 0.831, PLAAC 0.834, catGRANULE 0.817
  PdPS vs NoPS (ROC-AUC):  PScore 0.662, PLAAC 0.644, catGRANULE 0.706

  Human: hSaPS vs hNoPS:   PScore 0.813, PLAAC 0.831, catGRANULE 0.813
         hPdPS vs hNoPS:   PScore 0.689, PLAAC 0.640, catGRANULE 0.726

Average precision (PR-AUC) confirms the same asymmetry: for SaPS it is 9-18x
above the positive-class prevalence baseline (i.e., genuine top-of-list
enrichment), whereas for PdPS it is only ~2.6x above prevalence.

Head-to-head: for SaPS the three predictors are essentially equivalent (PLAAC
marginally best). For PdPS, catGRANULE is clearly the best (AUC 0.706/0.726),
followed by PScore, then PLAAC (0.644/0.640).

Conclusion: sequence-based PS predictors effectively detect self-assembling
phase-separating proteins but largely miss partner-dependent ones, which lack
the strong intrinsic disorder/prion-like signature and sit close to the non-PS
background. This shows current "PS prediction" mostly captures self-assembling
scaffolds and systematically under-detects partner-dependent condensate
components. The FuzDrop comparison requested in the prompt could not be
performed because FuzDrop scores are absent from the supplied data.

Major gaps include per-protein rather than global amino-acid frequency calculation, absence of any fold-change versus NoPS, and lack of a systematic property- or IDR-based ordering used for downstream analyses.

SLE expands classical monocytes similarly in both groups (16-19% to 27-29%; log2FC +0.60 European vs +0.78 Asian; interaction p = 0.64). This is the clearest ancestry-general SLE signature.

3) Suggestive but not robust ancestry differences: B cells fall in Europeans but not Asians (interaction p = 0.06 age-only, 0.19 batch-adjusted); plasmacytoid dendritic cells fall more in Europeans (log2FC -0.98 vs -0.18); progenitor cells fall more in Asians (rare 0.06% population, low confidence).

CONCLUSION: Asian SLE patients show a stronger CD4+ T-cell depletion and a stronger type-I interferon molecular response than European patients, while classical-monocyte expansion is shared. QUESTION: Can unsupervised clustering of hepatic transcriptomes stratify NAFLD patients by disease severity (fibrosis stage, NAS score, NASH stage, early/moderate grouping)?

ANSWER: Yes, but only weakly and not robustly — unsupervised clustering captures a modest fibrosis-severity signal, but it does not produce clean, reproducible severity strata, and it fails to stratify NAS score at the natural cluster solutions.

WHAT I DID
- Assembled raw HTSeq counts for 216 samples (64,253 Ensembl genes; 5 HTSeq summary rows dropped per file) and clinical metadata from the SOFT family file.
- Excluded the 10 healthy controls, leaving 206 NAFLD cases (NAFL 51, NASH_F0-F1 34, NASH_F2 53, NASH_F3 54, NASH_F4 14; fibrosis F0-F4; NAS 1-8).
- Filtered low-count genes (>=10 counts in >=20 samples), retaining 17,418 genes.
- Normalized with DESeq2 variance-stabilizing transformation (vst), cross-checked with edgeR TMM + log2 CPM.
- Took the top 2,000 most variable genes, z-scored per gene, then ran PCA and Ward hierarchical clustering (Euclidean), and tested clusters (k=2,3,4) against clinical features with Kruskal-Wallis, chi-square/Fisher exact, and Jonckheere-Terpstra trend tests.

KEY FINDINGS
1. The dominant transcriptomic axis is NOT severity. PC1 (30.9% of variance) correlates with library size (rho=0.48, p=3.8e-13) and is uncorrelated with fibrosis/NAS. The fibrosis/NAS gradient sits on PC2+PC3 (fibrosis rho +0.41 and -0.52; ~16% variance combined).
2. Cluster structure is weak: silhouette width is low at every k (max 0.21 at k=2).
3. Clusters differ in fibrosis stage and NASH group, but the association is modest:
   - k=2 (58 vs 148): fibrosis Kruskal-Wallis p=0.015, NASH-group chi2 p=0.019, but stage p=0.138 (n.s.) and NAS p=0.69 (n.s.).
   - k=3 (58/58/90): fibrosis p=0.020; group p=0.065 (n.s.); stage p=0.142 (n.s.); NAS p=0.75 (n.s.).
   - k=4 (21/37/58/90): fibrosis p=6.2e-5, group p=8.5e-4, stage p=0.0038, NAS p=0.005. Only here does a severity-enriched cluster (n=21) emerge, containing exclusively NASH_F2/F3/F4 with mean fibrosis 2.95 (vs 1.5-1.8) and mean NAS 5.76.
4. The k=4 result is NOT robust: its fibrosis p-value swings from 6e-5 to 0.31 depending on the number of variable genes (500-10000); cluster agreement between vst and TMM normalization is only ARI=0.62; and after removing the library-size (technical) component the k=4 cluster-fibrosis association disappears (p=0.96).
5. NAS score is poorly stratified overall: significant only at k=4 (p=0.005) and non-significant at k=2/3.

CONCLUSION
Unsupervised clustering of these hepatic transcriptomes recovers a real but secondary fibrosis-associated transcriptional program (PC2/PC3) and can surface a small advanced-disease subgroup (NASH F2-F4) at k=4. However, the cluster boundaries are unstable, the dominant variation is technical rather than severity-related, and NAS score is not reproducibly stratified. Therefore, for clinical-trial enrichment, whole-transcriptome unsupervised clustering of this cohort is insufficient on its own to define reliable molecular subtypes of NAFLD by disease severity.

LIMITATIONS
- Sex, age, and batch/centre are not provided in the metadata, so technical/batch confounding (including the library-size component) could not be fully controlled.
- No independent validation cohort or differential-expression/gene-set enrichment was performed; results are descriptive of GSE135251 only.
- "stage" (early/moderate) is a deterministic function of fibrosis stage, so those are not independent outcomes.
grader_notes: Work is strong except for missing multiple-testing correction and lack of explicit clinical-trial next step; all data processing and clustering are well documented.

QUESTION
How does gene expression in vastus lateralis skeletal muscle (SKM-VL) dynamically change over the 8-week endurance-training course in males and females, and what are the predominant sex-specific or shared temporal expression patterns?

ANSWER
Analyzing the 766 training-regulated transcripts (training_q < 0.05) measured in SKM-VL in males and females at 1w/2w/4w/8w (MoTrPAC endurance-training rat data):

1) Temporal dynamics — the response grows and peaks at 8 weeks in both sexes.
The number of timepoint-significant transcripts (timewise_p < 0.05 vs sex-matched sedentary controls) rises monotonically with training duration:
  Male:   1w=145 (85 up/60 down), 2w=134, 4w=176, 8w=379 (217 up/162 down)
  Female: 1w=220 (136 up/84 down), 2w=329, 4w=501, 8w=532 (342 up/190 down)
In both sexes the 8-week timepoint dominates, and the largest temporal archetype is "late-only" (significant at 4w/8w but not 1w/2w): 315 male, 287 female. Most remodelling therefore accumulates late in the course and is mildly biased toward up-regulation.

2) Predominant temporal patterns.
- Early (1–2w): a small, largely sex-specific acute response (only 47 male / 41 female genes are "early-only").
- Late (4–8w): the dominant, accumulating response ("late-only" genes).
- Sustained (significant both early and late): 145 male vs 329 female genes — more than twice as many in females. Another 259 male / 109 female genes are training-regulated overall but never reach individual-timepoint significance.
Only 161/766 (21%) genes share the exact same temporal pattern in both sexes.

3) Shared vs sex-specific response — divergent early, convergent late.
- Sex overlap of significant genes grows from 33 genes (Jaccard 0.10) at 1w to 265 genes (Jaccard 0.41) at 8w.
- Male–female logFC correlation rises from 0.13 (1w) to 0.63 (8w), and direction concordance among shared genes reaches ~100% at 8w (264/265).
- Overall: 402 genes are shared (significant in both sexes), 255 female-only, 105 male-only.
So the chronic (8-week) adaptation is largely shared and directionally concordant, whereas the acute (1–2 week) response is sex-divergent.

4) Biological content.
- Shared/sustained UP: mitochondrial/oxidative program — Ckmt1 (+3.75 male/+2.46 female; top shared gene), Ckmt2, Mpc2, Coq3, Sesn1, Mt-nd6, Tbc1d1, Il6r — consistent with oxidative-energy adaptation (creatine/phosphocreatine shuttle, mitochondrial metabolism).
- Shared/sustained DOWN: immediate-early transcription factors Fos and Egr1, plus Ldlr, Fbp2 — attenuation of the acute stress program with training.
- Sex-specific examples: Sln (sarcolipin) is male-specifically induced late (-1.21 at 1w to +2.44 at 8w) while remaining suppressed in females; male-specific Cda, Cfi, F2 (immune/coagulation) and Col1a1 (down); female-specific Znf750, Lamb3, Nr4a3.

5) Important caveat.
Females reach significance for more genes at every timepoint, but their timewise_logFC_se is systematically lower (8w: 0.138 vs 0.186), and male significant effects are larger (mean |logFC| 0.66 vs 0.47). The female gene-count excess therefore partly reflects higher statistical power, not necessarily a larger biological response; the most robust sex conclusions are the high directional concordance of the shared program and the specific sex-specific genes (e.g., Sln), not raw count differences.

Bottom line: SKM-VL gene expression is remodelled progressively over 8 weeks of endurance training, peaking at 8w; the early response is sex-specific while the late response converges on a shared, largely up-regulated oxidative/mitochondrial program, with a modest set of genuinely sex-specific genes (e.g., male-specific sarcolipin induction).
grader_notes: The agent correctly scoped the data and gave excellent biological interpretation, but failed the core requirement of requiring significance at all four timepoints per sex and did not encode 4-character directional patterns; thus criteria 2, 3, and 5 are deficient.

Union of the DMSO (GSM2715535) and AI-10-49 (GSM2715536) H3K27ac MACS2 peaks was merged
into 63,665 consensus regions; reads were counted per region in each BAM, normalized to
per-million mapped reads (DMSO 35,950,332; AI 37,332,216), and log2 fold change (AI/DMSO)

  -1.19; 76 regions lose >=4-fold). Of these, 3,829 are distal enhancers and 1,843 are

  are completely absent in AI-10-49 (no overlap with any AI peak), vs 10,156 gained -

  distal enhancers.

Interaction effect size between baseline insulin-resistance status and peak-glucose reduction (protein vs fiber pre-load on rice)

ANSWER:

There is a significant, large interaction between baseline insulin-resistance (IR) status and the magnitude of peak-glucose reduction achieved by a protein pre-load versus a fiber pre-load.

Metric definition: peak-glucose reduction = peak postprandial glucose after plain rice minus peak postprandial glucose after the pre-loaded rice meal (each subject is their own control). IR status from the insulin-suppression test SSPG (median split at 75 mg/dL; higher SSPG = more insulin resistant).

Interaction effect size (SSPG, n = 19):
- Linear mixed model (reduction ~ preload x IR + (1|subject)): interaction beta = -23.1 mg/dL (SE 9.3; 95% CI -41.4 to -4.8; p = 0.013); standardized interaction (beta / residual SD) = -1.61.
- Mixed 2x2 ANOVA: interaction F(1,17) = 6.14, p = 0.024, partial eta-squared = 0.265 (a large effect).
- Difference-in-differences (protein - fiber reduction): Cohen's d = -1.14, Hedges' g = -1.09.

Direction of the interaction:
- Insulin-sensitive participants: protein pre-load reduces the rice peak by ~24.9 mg/dL vs fiber ~6.6 mg/dL (protein - fiber = +18.4 mg/dL).
- Insulin-resistant participants: protein reduces the peak by only ~4.3 mg/dL vs fiber ~9.1 mg/dL (protein - fiber = -4.7 mg/dL).
So the protein pre-load's advantage over fiber in lowering the glucose peak is large in insulin-sensitive people and is abolished (directionally reversed) in insulin-resistant people.

Consistency/sensitivity:
- SSPG > 150 mg/dL threshold: interaction beta = -29.8 mg/dL (p = 0.008), partial eta-squared = 0.294, Hedges' g = -1.43.
- Continuous SSPG: interaction beta = -0.172 mg/dL per 1 mg/dL SSPG (p = 0.007); i.e. the protein-vs-fiber benefit falls by ~12.5 mg/dL per SD of SSPG.
- HOMA-IR median split (n = 23): same direction but smaller and not significant (Hedges' g = -0.63, p ~ 0.12).

Caveat: sample is small (n = 19 with SSPG; 4-15 or 9-10 per group), so the exact magnitude carries wide uncertainty; the HOMA-IR surrogate and baseline-corrected peaks show the same direction but weaker evidence.
grader_notes: The agent's analysis uses SSPG instead of DI for IR classification, raw peak instead of baseline-corrected peak, and consequently obtains significant, large interaction results that contradict the expected non-significant, negligible-effect pattern. Statistical methods and source citations are otherwise reasonable.

Interpretation: all three themes are gene programs that depend on ongoing protein secretion (cytokines, complement factors, ECM components, and secreted morphogens such as TGF-beta/WNT/Hedgehog), so their transcriptional suppression is the expected consequence of blocking ER-to-Golgi transport. This is reinforced by the complementary finding that HALLMARK_UNFOLDED_PROTEIN_RESPONSE is the single most strongly INDUCED pathway (mean NES +2.4, q < 0.004 in every cell type) — the direct ER-stress readout of secretory-pathway blockade. Together (UPR up + secretion-dependent programs down), the data confirm BFA's mechanism of action as a secretory-pathway disruptor.
grader_notes: The agent performed a reasonable GSEA analysis but deviated from the expected concentration-specific pre-ranked GSEA with padj < 0.05, using instead an aggregated per-cell-type mean log2FC ranking and FDR q < 0.25; consequently most criteria fall to B, while source reliability is strong.

MAPK pathway alterations are present in 66 of 669 (9.9%) post-hormonal-therapy HR+/HER2- tumors.

Interpretation
- Cumulative frequency = 66 / 669 = 9.87% (~9.9%).
- This is ~1.7-fold enriched versus treatment-naive HR+/HER2- primaries (38 / 657 = 5.8%; Fisher's exact two-sided p = 0.006; odds ratio 1.78), consistent with MAPK pathway activation as a mechanism of acquired endocrine resistance.

Shared genetic factor among metabolites (from the neonatal-metabolite GWAS summary statistics)

PRIMARY FINDING
The shared genetic factor is the medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase gene ACADM
(locus chr1:75,641,621-75,961,389, GRCh38; lead SNPs 75,727,547 / 75,727,809 /
75,736,585, all inside ACADM). This one locus is genome-wide significant
(p < 5e-8) and replication-consistent for FOUR acylcarnitine phenotypes:

  1. C6  (hexanoylcarnitine)          lead chr1:75,727,547 A>G  p=2.85e-13 (disc), p=1.90e-13 (repl)
  2. C8  (octanoylcarnitine)          lead chr1:75,736,585 G>T  p=1.82e-10 (disc), p=8.88e-17 (repl)
  3. C8/C2 (octanoyl-/acetylcarnitine ratio) lead chr1:75,727,547 A>G  p=6.30e-10 (disc), p=2.35e-19 (repl)
  4. (C3DC+C4-OH)/C10 (dicarboxy/hydroxy-acylcarnitines over decanoylcarnitine)
                                      lead chr1:75,727,809 A>C  p=1.18e-12 (disc), p=4.04e-12 (repl)

Evidence: 121 significant variants in the locus; 51 variants are significant for
all four traits at once; 97.8% (269/275) of the locus's variant-trait
associations replicate with concordant effect direction. C6, C8 and C8/C2 move
in the same direction (sign concordance 1.00), while the ratio trait is
anti-correlated (concordance 0.00) because its denominator C10 covaries with C8
(phenotypic C8-C10 Spearman r = 0.90). Across the full 20,474-variant panel the
effect sizes of C6 and C8 are strongly correlated (r = 0.81), the highest
between-trait pair, confirming shared genetic architecture.

SECONDARY (NOT ROBUST) CANDIDATE
A chr5:50,145,974-50,537,022 signal appears shared between C10:1 and C6DC in the
discovery cohort, but 0/58 of its variant-trait associations replicate
(all replication p > 0.45, sign-flipped), and it maps to a gene-poor region
(nearest protein-coding gene EMB ~200 kb away). It is therefore not considered
a confirmed shared factor.

OTHER METABOLITE LOCI ARE TRAIT-SPECIFIC (one gene per metabolite)
  C4         -> ACADS   (short-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase), chr12:120.7 Mb
  TYR        -> HPD     (4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase), chr12:121.9 Mb
  PRO        -> PRODH   (proline dehydrogenase 1),            chr22:18.9 Mb
  C8:1       -> ACSM2A  (acyl-CoA synthetase medium-chain 2A),chr16:20.5 Mb
  C4DC+C5-OH -> CRAT    (carnitine O-acetyltransferase),      chr9:129.1 Mb
  C6DC       -> CPT2    (carnitine palmitoyltransferase 2),   chr1:53.2 Mb
  C10:1      -> CYP4A11, chr1:46.9 Mb
  C0         -> chr11:68.6 Mb (and a non-replicating chr15 signal)

INTERPRETATION
ACADM encodes the enzyme that catalyzes the first step of medium-chain fatty-acid
beta-oxidation. Variation at this locus coordinately shifts medium-chain
acylcarnitines (C6, C8 and their ratios), which is why a single genetic factor
shows up for several metabolites simultaneously; the extreme biallelic loss of
function is medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency (MCADD, OMIM 201450),
the classic acylcarnitine-profile disorder of newborn screening.

LIMITATIONS
Gene identity at each locus is inferred (nearest/best-matching gene), not proven;
no LD reference was available so loci were clustered by a 500 kb distance proxy;
ratio traits partly inherit the genetic signal of their component metabolites.
grader_notes: The agent conducted a GWAS replication-based shared-locus analysis rather than the meta-analysis and colocalization pipeline expected by the rubric; core meta-analysis and colocalization criteria are therefore unmet, while locus identification and source reliability are strong.

Genomic landscape across breast-cancer receptor subtypes (MSK-IMPACT, n=1,806 samples)

Cohort: HR+HER2- n=1,422 (79%), HR+HER2+ n=141 (8%), HR-HER2+ n=66 (4%), TNBC n=177 (10%). Subtype taken from the primary-tumor receptor annotation; 112 samples with unknown/equivocal status were excluded. All frequencies are per-sample percentages; p-values are chi-square/Fisher with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction.

1) Somatic (non-silent) mutation landscape
- TP53 mutation rises steadily toward the aggressive/basal end: HR+HER2- 26.9% -> HR+HER2+ 45.4% -> HR-HER2+ 78.8% -> TNBC 89.8% (p=2.7e-71). Near-universal TP53 loss is a hallmark of TNBC and HER2-enriched disease.
- PIK3CA is a luminal marker: 41.1% (HR+HER2-), 38.3% (HR+HER2+), 25.8% (HR-HER2+), but only 14.1% in TNBC (depleted, p=7.1e-13). AKT1 (6.3%) and PTEN mutation (7.2%) further activate the PI3K/AKT axis in HR+HER2-.
- Luminal/ER-program genes are confined to HR+ disease: GATA3 (17.5%/17.0%, 0% in HR- subtypes), CDH1 (19.1% in HR+HER2-), MAP3K1 (9.0%), TBX3 (5.3%), CBFB (5.2%), and ESR1 (8.5-9.9% in HR+, ~0% elsewhere) - the latter marking acquired endocrine resistance.
- TNBC instead carries tumor-suppressor loss: RB1 mutation 9.6% (p=6.2e-6), PIK3R1 7.3%, plus modest BRCA1 (2.8%)/BRCA2 (4.5%) mutations (homologous-recombination defect subset). HR-HER2+ uniquely enriches NF1 (12.1%, p=9.2e-3).

2) Copy-number landscape
- ERBB2 amplification is the defining event of both HER2+ groups: 66.7% (HR+HER2+) and 86.4% (HR-HER2+), vs 1.5% HR+HER2- and 1.1% TNBC (p=2.1e-237), with 17q12 co-amplification of CDK12 (50-56%).
- HR+ (luminal) tumors enrich CCND1 (21%), the 11q13 amplicon FGF3/FGF4/FGF19 (~17-19%), FGFR1 (13%), and MDM2 (4.8%) amplifications - all largely absent from TNBC.
- TNBC enriches MYC amplification (16.4%, p=2.9e-4) and deep deletions of PTEN (5.6%, p=2.6e-3) and RB1 (6.2%, p=1.6e-6).

3) Tumor mutation burden
- Low and similar across subtypes (median 0.10-0.13 mut/Mb). No significant overall difference (Kruskal-Wallis p=0.091); TNBC is only marginally higher than HR+HER2- (nominal p=0.016, FDR q=0.097).

Bottom line: The subtypes segregate into distinct genomic groups - (i) HR+HER2- is a PI3K/AKT-ER-pathway-driven luminal disease (PIK3CA/AKT1/PTEN, GATA3/CDH1/MAP3K1, ESR1, CCND1/FGFR1 amplifications); (ii) HR+HER2+ combines this luminal/PI3K axis with ERBB2/CDK12 amplification and higher TP53; (iii) HR-HER2+ is the most amplicon-driven, TP53-high group with NF1 loss; and (iv) TNBC is defined by near-universal TP53 mutation plus RB1/PTEN inactivation, MYC amplification, and low PIK3CA activation. These differences reveal actionable subcohorts: PI3K/AKT inhibitors and ESR1/FGFR1/CDK4-6 targeting in HR+ disease, anti-HER2 (+CDK12) in HER2+ tumors, and PARP inhibitors in the BRCA1/2-mutant TNBC subset.

Limitations: sample-level (not patient-level) analysis of a targeted ~470-gene panel; subtype assigned from primary-tumor annotation (minor receptor discordance in metastases); HR-HER2+ group is small (n=66) so rare-event power is limited; descriptive, without treatment/outcome association.
grader_notes: The agent performs a comprehensive and statistically rigorous analysis of the data, correctly loading and linking datasets and classifying subtypes; it excels at driver gene and TMB analysis, but falls short on ERBB2 point mutation separation and some interpretive points regarding rare ERBB2 mutations and TMB significance.
